1:
Matthew Henry puts the envy in the first person, as the thought a man must not let in: that he might shake off the restraints of religion and conscience and take the same liberty with his appetites that he sees others take. He finds a second reason in the verse that follows, that not only the end of such men is bad but the way—their heart studies destruction for others and will prove destruction to themselves—so they are to be looked at not with envy but with pity, or a just indignation at what they do. John Gill lists what already attends them, woe and sorrow, wounds and strife, with poverty to follow, and takes the studied destruction three ways: aimed at the good men who reprove them, at drawing others into their methods, and in the end unwittingly at themselves, since the intemperance they plan is their own ruin. Keil and Delitzsch ground the warning in the risk of partnership: whoever keeps such company makes himself a sharer in greater sins, the heart of these men brooding violence—robbery, plunder, murder—while the second noun means the trouble they prepare for others by slanderous and uncharitable talk. John Wesley reduces it to how they may oppress and destroy.

The turn to the house built by wisdom is read as the answer to that envy. Wesley makes the connection explicit: there is no need to raise a family by ruining others, since wisdom will do it more effectually. Henry works the same argument at length. A man may raise his estate by lawful means with a good conscience and a good name, and if the unjust man is raised a little sooner, the honest man’s house lasts a great deal longer; men may build by unrighteous practices but cannot establish, the foundation being rotten, whereas what is honestly got will wear like steel. He is careful about what the wisdom is: both piety towards God, which is true wisdom, and prudence in managing outward affairs, since some who are truly pious do not thrive for want of prudence and some prudent enough do not prosper because they lean to their own understanding.

The chambers filled with precious and pleasant riches are given both a literal and a spiritual reading, and most of the commentators want both. Henry keeps the two adjectives apart—precious because the riches were got by honest labour, pleasant because they are enjoyed with holy cheerfulness—while noting that some take the verse chiefly of spiritual riches, the chambers of the soul filled with the graces and comforts of the Spirit. Gill takes the literal sense first, the private rooms as well as the shops, warehouses, barns and granaries filled by improved trade or husbandry, then turns it to the fulness the church has from Christ and the treasures of wisdom laid up in a believer. He does the same with the house itself, applying it to a family raised by prudent management, to the church built by Wisdom, and to a man’s own soul built on the one foundation. Charles Ellicott puts the double sense in a line, that the riches are not only earthly wealth but the true riches, the knowledge and love of God, and Wesley glosses the knowledge as including the love and practice of what we know. Adam Clarke keeps to the domestic sense, taking the house for a family and its affairs; his fuller contribution here is the chapter argument, laying out in order the topics to come—the house wisely built, counsel in war, saving life while one can, the honey and the honeycomb, the just man who falls seven times, the ruin of the wicked, and the field of the sluggard. Keil and Delitzsch mark the same structure more briefly, that the praise of wisdom now continues by showing it brings blessing in peace and victory in war.
5:
The strength of the wise man is variously illustrated. Adam Clarke makes it mechanical: wisdom enables a man to construct machines by which he can do the labour of a hundred or a thousand men; and he cites a Greek rendering preferring the wise man to the strong and the prudent to a stout husbandman. John Gill borrows the Stoic praise of their wise man, that he is happy and rich and mighty and even a king, and claims it more truly for the good man—though his strength is comparative, being greatest when he knows himself weak. John Wesley keeps it plain: wisdom does greater things than strength can. On the counsel that wins wars, Gill lays out what a state should weigh first, the justice of its cause, the sufficiency of men and money, the method of attack or defence, and above all God’s counsel; Charles Ellicott and Wesley carry the point into the spiritual warfare, where the end aimed at and the means of reaching it both need advising.

The saying that wisdom is too high for a fool produces a philological quarrel. Keil and Delitzsch report the usual rendering—that the way to wisdom is too long and steep, the price too costly to afford—and grant the thought is near the poet’s; but they object that it leaves the plural form of the noun unexplained, and prefer to make wisdom seem to the fool an ornamental commodity above his station. Matthew Henry takes the received sense and divides it: the fool thinks wisdom too high and so, despairing, takes no pains; and really it is too high, for he has not the capacity. Wisdom is no easy thing to get, and men of good parts miss it by being slothful, or trifling, or given to pleasure, or in bad company. Gill allows both the natural and the spiritual reach of the words, and thinks the difficulty may lie in the man’s own opinion as much as in fact. On the silence in the gate Henry is sharpest: such men are not admitted to the council, or if they are they sit as dumb statues and stand for cyphers, saying nothing because they have nothing to say. Ellicott adds the reason, that he was too self-willed to learn and must stay sheepishly silent while others give their opinion; Clarke says only that he is not put into offices of trust; Wesley, that he cannot speak profitably in a public assembly.

The last pair concerns contriving rather than doing, and here the readings divide. Gill and Wesley take the thought itself to be sin—the motions of sin in the mind are forbidden by the commandment against coveting, and the inward contrivance of evil is sin in God’s sight. Clarke draws a line: a simple thought about foolishness, or about sin itself, is not sinful; what is criminal is the purpose, the harbouring of evil thoughts and the devising how to sin. Ellicott sides with the second, rendering it that sin is the contrivance of self-will. Keil and Delitzsch supply the philology, since the noun comes from a root meaning to contrive and denotes the marshalling of thoughts towards an end, particularly the refined preparation of a sinful act. Henry holds both ends: he grants that devising evil is made light of and turned off as a merely foolish thing, and answers that it is sin, and you cannot call it by a worse name—it is bad to do evil but worse to devise it. On the title such a man earns, Gill catalogues the inventions, new sins or new methods of sinning, new oaths and games and ways of cheating; Henry supposes master of mischief was then a common name of reproach; Keil and Delitzsch note that such definitions have no lexicographical but only a moral aim, warning a man against earning the ambiguous name of a cunning one.
10:
The fainting in the day of adversity is read as diagnosis rather than reproach. Keil and Delitzsch take the first clause as a supposition and the second as the conclusion a man must draw about himself: if he shows himself remiss, changeable, timorous, unable to resist when difficulty comes, he has pronounced his own verdict. They point to the play on words between the strait and the strength—if the strength is pressed together and bowed down at the very moment it ought to expand, it is a limited strength and its owner a weakling—and quote a rendering generalising it: he is not strong who is not firm in need. Matthew Henry describes the state before judging it: the spirits sink, the hands hang down, the knees grow feeble, and those most cheerful in health often droop most when anything ails them; some are so feeble that if a trouble does but threaten them they faint at once, unfitting themselves to grapple with it. His verdict is that this argues want of resolution, consideration and faith, which is the strength of a soul; his remedy, that a man of good courage will find God strengthening his heart. Adam Clarke renders the last words as a contracting of the strength and adds that in trial we should be doubly courageous, since a man who loses courage finds his strength avails him nothing. Charles Ellicott notes that the verse leaves a man unable to help himself or others, and that a more excellent way follows.

That verse is a command, and they are careful about its grammar and its scope. Keil and Delitzsch note that the passage runs to six lines rather than the usual two, and reject the reading that makes the opening particle an oath—forbear not, I adjure thee—since the parallelism wants both classes of victim as objects of a single imperative, deliver, which all the old interpreters read as an imperative and none as an infinitive. Ellicott renders it that way outright. John Gill widens the class to be delivered: men taken by robbers, like the traveller the priest and Levite passed by; men unjustly sentenced, whom one who knows their innocence should save by testimony, intercession or counsel, as friends did for Joseph, for David and for the prophet; and men drawn into snares of immorality or heresy. Henry widens it further, to any exposing themselves through ignorance—travellers on the road, ships at sea—and insists the duty holds towards those we owe no particular obligation, out of a general zeal for justice, and holds even at peril to ourselves. Clarke puts the negative sharply: a man who through any pretence neglects to save one unjustly condemned is guilty of blood.

The excuse is answered by all of them, Henry giving it the fullest hearing before demolishing it. He grants the plea is easy to make and hard to disprove, since no one can contradict a man who says he did not know or had forgotten, and observes that the temptation to lie is strongest where the truth lies wholly in one’s own breast. But the same plea will not stand a second court. God ponders the heart and keeps the soul—which Henry turns into a reason for tenderness towards other lives, since our own have been precious in his sight—and knows whether the ignorance was real or the true cause was that we did not love our neighbour; and he renders to every man according to his works, counting omissions of good as well as commissions of evil. Gill lists the forms the excuse takes, that we did not know the danger, or the innocence, or what to do, or that it lay in our power, and reports a version reading that our strength was not sufficient. Ellicott hears behind it the oldest evasion, whether a man is his brother’s keeper; John Wesley dismisses it as frivolous.
13:
The honey draws unusually first-hand interest. Adam Clarke insists on the comb: the flavour is finer in it than after the honey is pressed out and exposed to the air; and to the claim that the comb is never eaten he answers that only a man with no acquaintance with an apiary could say so, having seen it eaten often and eaten it himself—and no one who has not can feel the force of the scriptural allusions to it. John Gill adds its dietary and medical reputation, that honey nourishes and heals and is said to prolong the lives of those who use it much. Matthew Henry turns the taste into an argument: those who have tasted honey need no proof that it is sweet and cannot be argued out of it, and so those who have experienced the power of truth and godliness are proof against all the sophistry of atheists and the banter of the profane. He presses the difference—honey may be sweet and yet not wholesome, whereas wisdom has a future recompence as well as a present sweetness, so that the servants of sin pay dearly for their pains while wisdom pays for its own. John Wesley notes that the eating is not commanded but conceded, standing there only to illustrate what follows.

What follows turns on one noun, and Clarke makes the most of it. He denies that the word ever means recompense, since its root refers to what is behind, after, or last in time and never carries the idea of compensation; the sense is that there is another state or life, and a man’s expectation of happiness in a future world shall not be cut off. He supports this by running through seven versions, ancient and English, and showing that not one understood it as a reward. Charles Ellicott agrees on the philology, glossing it literally as a future, and would recast the first clause to say that a man should know wisdom to be as sweet and good for his soul. Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way. Gill and Wesley keep the received sense and its consolation, Gill making the wisdom the knowledge of Christ, sweeter than any other, and Wesley saying it is not only sweet for the present but brings a sure and everlasting reward.

The threat against the righteous man’s house raises a real dispute about what his falling means. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the warning is aimed not at his person but at his dwelling and resting-place, forbidding a man to covet his house and drive him out by cunning or violence; they note that two old translators misread a word here and produced a sense without sense. Henry says the words are spoken less as counsel to wicked men, who will not take instruction, than in defiance of them for the encouragement of the good, whose enemies lie in wait at the door and expect to succeed because he is weak. Then comes the question of the seven falls. Ellicott is flat that it means falls into trouble and not into sin, as is often supposed, so malice is useless against a man God protects; Wesley and Clarke read it so too, Clarke adding that though violence spoil his tent and affliction press his body, he emerges each time from the furnace brighter and more refined. Gill will not choose, holding that the just fall into both troubles and sins, each causing the other, and that both senses may be kept, though the first suits the context better. Henry takes both and then decides: the man falls into trouble and rises, and falls into sins of infirmity and rises by repentance, like a traveller who stumbles at a stone and gets up to go on with more care—but the verse, he concludes, is rather to be understood of falls into affliction than into actual sin.
17:
The prohibition on gloating is qualified by nearly all of them alike. John Gill allows joy at the fall of the public enemies of God, as when a nation sang at the drowning of its oppressor or as the church is called to rejoice at the fall of antichrist, partly for their own deliverance and chiefly for the glory of God’s justice—refusing it only where private revenge is the motive. Matthew Henry draws the same line: there may be holy joy in the destruction of God’s enemies as it makes for his glory and the church’s welfare, but in the ruin of our enemies as ours we must by no means rejoice, and must rather weep with them when they weep, without so much as letting the heart be secretly glad. He is sharp about the secret delight itself, the Aha with which a corrupt heart greets a rival’s stumble. Adam Clarke makes it a rule of the affections: God will not have a man avenge himself or feel any disposition contrary to love.

The threat attached is read as a transfer of punishment. Clarke takes the wrath for its effect, so that God may take the punishment off the enemy and lay it on the man who gloats—or inflict a like punishment, since whoever gets into that spirit deserves it. Charles Ellicott says the same in a clause, that the wrath turns on the rejoicer as having sinned more deeply than his enemy; John Wesley notes that the Hebrew phrase implies the upon thee the English leaves out. Henry supplies the domestic picture: it displeases God as it displeases a prudent father to see one child triumph in the correction of another, which he ought rather to tremble at and take warning by. He then turns it into an argument a man cannot answer—he can do his fallen enemy no greater kindness than to rejoice at his fall, since the wrath of man does not work the righteousness of God, and the righteousness of God was never meant to gratify the wrath of man.

On the repeated warning against envy, Gill observes that its frequency suggests good men are prone to the fault, and that the wording is borrowed from a psalm of the writer’s father. Keil and Delitzsch diagnose short-sightedness: the anger at what looks like an unjust division of fortune, and the jealousy at the success the godless enjoy, both come of regarding the present and not the end. Ellicott calls it the difficulty that troubled the psalmist. Henry adds the corrective, that even what grieves us must not fret us, and our eye must not be evil against anyone because God is good—are we wiser or juster than he? The reason given divides on one noun. Ellicott renders it literally as a future, and Clarke takes the same line, that there shall be no future state of blessedness for the wicked, with a caution against pressing it too far: some have thought the words hint at the annihilation of sinners, but they refer not to being, only to the state of that being—the wicked shall be, but shall not be happy. Gill canvasses the possibilities: no good end, or no hope of future things as one version has it, or no posterity, the word being sometimes used of offspring. Henry keeps it simple: a prosperity serving only for present subsistence is all such a man will ever get, nothing being intended for him in the world of retribution, and his candle shines brightly only to be presently put out. Clarke also uses his note here to look back at the preceding verse and attack the reading that makes the just man’s seven falls seven daily sins: sin is not named in the text, day is in neither the Hebrew nor any version, and the verb is never used of falling into sin but always into distress.
21:
The pairing of God and the king is handled carefully by all of them. John Gill insists on the order—first the Lord, then the king, who stands under him and is to be feared with a fear suitable to a man, in everything consistent with the fear of God. Matthew Henry makes religion and loyalty inseparable: those truly religious will be loyal in conscience towards God, the godly in the land will be the quiet in the land, and how should a man be true to his prince who is false to his God?—while adding that where the two come into competition the case is adjudged, and we must obey God rather than men. Adam Clarke distributes the homage, divine adoration to the one and civil obedience to the other.

The second clause divides them. Henry insists on the exact wording: it does not say have nothing to do with those that change, for there may be cause to change for the better, but with those given to change, who affect change for its own sake out of a peevish discontent with what is, a fondness for novelty, or a wish to fish in troubled waters. Clarke renders them changelings, the innovators who are always making experiments on forms of government and of religion, and calls that the most dangerous spirit that can infect the human mind. Charles Ellicott quietly offers another sense altogether, that the phrase may mean those who think differently, and John Wesley a third, that they are men unstable in their obedience to God or the king. On the calamity that follows, Henry observes that restless and factious spirits commonly pull mischief on their own heads before they are aware, and that designs carried on with the utmost secrecy are discovered notwithstanding; Gill applies it to those who bring in damnable heresies and cry peace while destruction is coming; Clarke and Ellicott divide the two ruins between rebels against God and rebels against the king.

At the twenty-third verse the book changes hands, or seems to. Clarke thinks a new section begins and that what follows may belong to another collection, fragments of sayings gathered by wise men. Ellicott takes the phrase to mean simply that the wise are the authors of what follows. Gill reports the same rendering—that these are the sayings of wise men, other than Solomon, of his time or later—but thinks it more than probable that the rest of the chapter is Solomon’s own. Wesley only insists that the counsels to the end of the chapter deserve as much consideration as what came before. The subject is partiality on the bench, and Keil and Delitzsch explain the two Hebrew idioms for it, lifting the face and regarding the face, the partisan looking with pleasure on one man’s countenance or setting one person before another in his sight. Henry draws the portrait: a good judge will know the truth and not know faces, neither countenancing a friend in a bad cause nor omitting anything that could be said for a righteous cause because it happens to be an enemy’s. He extends the duty from magistrates to ministers, whose business it is to show men their transgressions—so that when such a man instead palliates the wickedness, or worse, prefers the wicked man and keeps his company, which is in effect to call him righteous, the people will curse him and even foreigners abhor him as a base betrayer of his trust. Gill adds the limit that keeps the saying practicable: the verse is not about a private opinion, which might be mistaken or merely flattering, but about a sentence pronounced in open court, where the wicked are justified for reward.
25:
The kiss on the lips has been construed several ways, and Keil and Delitzsch canvass them. The old versions make someone kiss the lips of the man who answers rightly, which they think forces the words; another takes the verb as passive, which the form will not bear; a third has the lips kiss him who answers. Taking the participle as subject gives the plain sense, that he who kisses the lips is the man giving an excellent answer—the lips being those the answer concerns. Charles Ellicott reaches the same construction and gives it a memorable turn: his words are as pleasant as if he had kissed the inquirer’s lips. John Gill keeps the received English and asks who is meant, a witness answering aptly or a judge pronouncing sentence, and notes that a kiss signifies both affection and obedience; Adam Clarke and John Wesley reduce it to affection and respect. On the verse before, Gill and Wesley agree that the rebuke is the public and judicial kind, the delight being the rebuker’s own good conscience, the people’s satisfaction, or God’s.

The advice about preparing the work outside is taken first as economics. Matthew Henry makes it a rule of household management: prefer necessaries to conveniences, do not lay out on show what should support the family, be content with a mean cottage rather than go into debt, and do not build until you can afford to. Many have ruined estate and family by spending on what brings nothing in and building when they could not finish; and some, he notes, take the verse as advice to a young man not to marry until he can keep a household. He adds the general principle, that a great design should be fully prepared for before it is begun, so the work does not stand still for want of materials—as when the temple was built and all was made ready before it came to the ground. Keil and Delitzsch make it a warning against setting up a household before the conditions are met: finish what a husbandman’s calling requires, then build. Clarke reduces it to doing nothing without a plan, preparing seed and implements in winter against seed-time and harvest, and Ellicott carries the method into the spiritual life, where a man should learn what he ought to do rather than waste energy on unattainable objects.

The last two verses concern restraint in law, and Henry is the most searching. As a witness a man must not testify without cause, nor deceive the court or his acquaintance into an ill opinion of his neighbour—speaking what is true is not enough if the manner of speaking insinuates otherwise, so that he deceives by innuendo or hyperbole. As a plaintiff he must not proceed from revenge, since even a righteous cause becomes unrighteous when prosecuted with malice; and to render to a man according to his work is God’s prerogative, so whoever carves for himself forfeits his appeal to that tribunal. Keil and Delitzsch define the phrase precisely: not a witness ignorant of the facts but one with no substantial reason for testifying at all—and allow themselves an aside on an old grammarian’s derivation, that the ancients, knowing nothing of the laws of sound, thought anything possible. Clarke warns against volunteering testimony in revenge; Ellicott, against mentioning a neighbour’s faults from malice or gossip. On the refusal of retaliation they grant that in public justice like for like is the nearest form of punishment, but observe that even the old law did not stop at external retortion, practicable only for injuries to person and property, and put in its place an atonement measured by a higher standard—while on purely moral grounds the principle has no validity at all. Ellicott calls the verse a wonderful anticipation of a later teaching, and Gill, that private revenge is sinful in itself and worse in its methods.
30:
All of them treat the passage as a parable from observation. John Gill thinks it very probably a matter of fact, the king’s road running past the field of a man who never went into it himself, and takes the neglected ground for an emblem of the unregenerate heart, unbroken and impenitent, where the seed of the word lies as if fallen by the wayside. Matthew Henry notices that the observation was accidental: the king did not go on purpose but looked as he passed, which he says is proper for travellers and for magistrates alike, and saw good soil overrun—not a thorn here and there but the whole of it—and no wall left to keep the fruit if there had been any. He turns this into praise of the husbandman’s calling, without which the earth would be a wilderness: the king himself is served by the field, and would be ill served if God did not teach the ploughman discretion. Keil and Delitzsch describe the form rather than the scene, a proverbial ode of the slothful cast as a record of experience, closing the supplement, and note the customary trick of distinguishing classes of men by two words for man. Charles Ellicott supplies the spiritual application, warning against letting the weeds of evil habits grow in the garden of the soul, or the wall of God’s protection be taken down for want of constant prayer.

Adam Clarke gives the fullest treatment, much of it social rather than exegetical. Borrowing from an earlier commentator, he observes that agriculture was then honourable and no man respected who let his ground go, that the law prevented the rich from utterly depressing the poor by returning farms and remitting debts at the appointed years, and that in that commonwealth one never sees the suddenly raised fortunes which cannot subsist but in the ruin of numberless families. He adds that the Romans thought it no mean praise to call a man a good husbandman, since from such men they drew their best generals; and he cannot resist the comparison with his own country, where the merchant is all in all, though the sea is not more uncertain than property got that way.

Clarke analyses the parable under five heads: the owner, a loitering man wanting heart, void of courage and decision; his estate, arable ground and a vineyard that might be orchard and garden; its condition, neglected long enough for brambles to grow even in the fields, nettles covering its face, nothing pruned or dug, the fence fallen for want of repair; the effect on the observer, who fixed his attention on it as no mere report but a thing seen, put his heart on it, took an intellectual view and so received a lesson, while the owner alone learnt nothing, hugging himself in his sloth; and the consequences, poverty coming like a traveller a few steps nearer the door each hour, and want like an armed man—or, he suggests, a man coming with an execution into the house, armed with the law, to take even the bed from under the slumberer. Henry draws the same lesson from the observer’s conduct: he did not break out into passionate censure or call the man ill names, but set himself to profit by what he saw; those who instruct others must first receive instruction, and it may be had not only from what we read and hear but from what we see, and not only from men’s good manners but their bad—which he supports with an old saying that wise men profit more by fools than fools by wise men, since the wise avoid the faults of fools while fools will not imitate the virtues of the wise. Gill supplies the sluggard’s own voice, craving one more doze instead of rising; John Wesley the moral in a phrase, that he learned wisdom by another’s folly.
